title: Request Latency Decomposition
description: Break down where an HTTP request spends its time in ASP.NET Core, from Kestrel and middleware to routing, controllers, database calls, and JSON serialization.

data.text: Every API request passes through many layers before returning a response. When a request takes 500 milliseconds, you need to know whether that time is spent in network calls, database queries, serialization, or middleware. **Request latency decomposition** is the practice of measuring each layer so you can target the real bottleneck instead of guessing.
The Layers of an ASP.NET Core Request

A typical request flows through Kestrel, middleware, routing, the controller action, authorization filters, database access, model binding, and JSON serialization. Each layer adds some overhead. In high-throughput APIs, serialization alone can consume 20–30% of request time.

terms.definition: The cross-platform web server that hosts ASP.NET Core applications and processes raw HTTP requests.
Software components that form a pipeline to handle requests and responses, such as authentication, caching, and CORS.
The process that converts HTTP request data into .NET objects that controller actions can use.
Converting .NET objects into JSON or another format for the HTTP response body.

data.title: Timing Middleware
data.content: Add a simple timing middleware to log how long each request takes end-to-end.

data.text: ASP.NET Core already creates an `Activity` for each request. You can listen to `Activity.Start`, `Activity.Stop`, and custom diagnostic events to measure specific phases. The framework emits events for routing, model binding, and action execution that you can correlate with performance counters.

data.title: Diagnostic Listener for Action Execution
data.content: Create a listener that tracks how long controller actions take independently of the full request pipeline.

data.title: Avoid Adding Too Many Timers
data.text: Every Stopwatch and log statement adds overhead. In production, use sampling or conditional logging so your observability tools do not become the performance problem they are meant to solve.

The biggest wins usually come from database and external HTTP calls. Entity Framework Core exposes `DiagnosticListener` events for query execution time. For HTTP calls, use `IHttpClientFactory` with delegating handlers to capture request and response durations without scattering timing code throughout your application.

data.title: Quick Wins
items: Enable EF Core interceptors to log query execution time and parameter values.
Use `IHttpClientFactory` so you can add a single delegating handler for timing all outbound calls.
Check JSON serializer settings: camelCase and reference handling can add milliseconds per request.
Measure response compression savings on large payloads with `ResponseCompression` middleware.

data.title: Key Takeaway
points: Latency decomposition isolates each layer: server, middleware, routing, controller, and I/O.
Use middleware, Activity listeners, or EF Core interceptors to measure specific phases.
Focus on database and external calls first—they usually dominate total request time.
Keep measurement overhead low with sampling and conditional logging.
data.takeaway: Measure first, optimize second. Without data, you are just guessing where the time goes.
